source_text: Domine ne in furore tuo arguas me. Reprehensio verbo fit; qui iugo praeceptoris non subditur ira Dei castigatur — castigatio reprehensione molestior.
thought_title: Rebuke by word and chastisement by wrath
orientation: Origen is beginning his homily on Psalm 37, quoting the psalmist's opening plea to the Lord and distinguishing verbal rebuke from the harsher chastisement of God's anger.
pass_a_gloss: Lord [do] not in fury your rebuke me. Rebuke by word happens; [he] who to [the] yoke of [the] teacher not is subjected [by the] anger of God is chastised — chastisement [than] rebuke more troublesome.

choices.why: The glossary distinguishes rebuke as verbal reproof, and the psalmist's plea is for God not to rebuke in fury.
The glossary gives 'rebuke' for reprehensio, and Origen immediately defines it as happening by word.
The glossary gives 'chastisement' for castigatio, and Origen contrasts it as more severe than verbal rebuke.
The image of the teacher's yoke is kept literally, since Origen is explaining who falls under God's chastising anger.
The comparative force is preserved, since Origen is ranking chastisement above rebuke in severity.

bible_refs.note: Domine ne in furore tuo arguas me

pass_b_english: "Lord, do not rebuke me in your fury" (Psalm 37:1 (LXX 36:1)). A rebuke happens by word; the one who does not submit to the yoke of the teacher is chastised by the anger of God—and chastisement is more grievous than rebuke.
